title: Beyond diesel: Multi‐objective optimization and multi‐criteria evaluation of hybrid multi‐energy systems for remote northern communities
content:
Abstract

Remote northern communities in Canada rely heavily on diesel-based electricity and heating, resulting in high energy costs, greenhouse gas emissions, and fuel-supply vulnerabilities. This study develops an integrated techno-economic framework for the design and evaluation of hybrid multi-energy systems (HMES) comprising solar photovoltaic (PV), wind turbines, an organic Rankine cycle (ORC)-based biomass-fired combined heat and power (BCHP) unit, battery energy storage, and power converters. A multi-objective optimization approach is employed to minimize the net present cost (NPC) and levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), while TOPSIS-SOMIT-based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is used to rank candidate system configurations. An off-grid community in a remote northern region of Canada, with an average daily electricity demand of 8,536 kWh, was selected as the case study. The optimal HMES comprises a 450 kW ORC-BCHP unit, 350 kW of PV capacity, 460 kW of wind capacity, and 2,200 kWh of battery storage, with an initial capital investment of C$13.5 million. The optimized system achieves an LCOE of C$0.458/kWh and an NPC of C$27.1 million. It generates 3,307 MWh of electricity annually, fully meeting community demand while eliminating 821,600 L/year of diesel consumption. Lifecycle CO2 emissions decrease from 0.704 to 0.076 kg/kWh, representing an 89% reduction. TOPSIS-SOMIT-based MCDA ranks the proposed HMES as the preferred option among seven candidate systems. The results indicate that integrating dispatchable biomass cogeneration with wind, solar, and battery storage can provide a reliable, cost-effective, and low-carbon energy solution for remote northern communities.
